title: Assess the Effectiveness of Software Security
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 8: Software Development Security: Assess the Effectiveness of Software Security.

rows: Analyzes source code without executing it; white-box approach
Tests running application from the outside; black-box approach
Combines SAST and DAST; instruments the application to monitor from inside during testing
Embedded within the application; monitors and protects in real-time during production

blocks.text: Each testing approach has strengths and limitations: SAST — Analyzes source code or bytecode to find vulnerabilities without executing the program. Advantages: can find issues early, covers all code paths. Limitations: high false positive rate, language-dependent, cannot find runtime issues. DAST — Tests the running application by sending requests and analyzing responses. Advantages: finds runtime vulnerabilities, language-independent, tests the application as an attacker would. Limitations: limited code coverage, cannot identify the specific vulnerable code, slower. IAST — Combines elements of both SAST and DAST by instrumenting the application. As the CBK notes, "like code analysis like SAST, it is also language-dependent, meaning some languages may not be supported and the dynamic elements of IAST may cause performance issues if run in a production environment." RASP — "As the name implies, RASP is designed to run inside an application in real time, providing continuous security monitoring and protection." It can detect and block attacks as they occur, providing a last line of defense. ⚠️ Exam Trap: SAST = white box (analyzes source code, no execution needed). DAST = black box (tests running application, no source code needed). Know when to use each: SAST during development, DAST against deployed applications, RASP in production.

items: Fuzz testing (fuzzing) — sending random, unexpected, or malformed input to an application to find crashes, exceptions, or security vulnerabilities
Two main approaches:
Mutation (dumb) fuzzing — takes valid input and randomly modifies it (bit flipping, inserting random data)
Generational (intelligent/smart) fuzzing — develops data models and creates new fuzzed input based on understanding of the data types used by the program
Effective at finding: buffer overflows, format string vulnerabilities, injection flaws, denial of service conditions
Automated and can run continuously; produces large volumes of test cases
Limited by code coverage — may not reach all code paths

blocks.text: Fuzzing is a powerful technique for finding security vulnerabilities that traditional testing methods might miss. Mutation fuzzing is simpler to set up — it takes known good inputs and randomly modifies them. Generational fuzzing is more sophisticated — it understands the input format and generates test cases that are more likely to trigger edge cases. Key exam points:

items: Mutation fuzzing = takes existing valid data and randomly modifies it
Generational fuzzing = creates new data based on understanding of the expected input format
Generational fuzzing is more effective but requires more setup (understanding the input specification)
Both approaches are useful for finding vulnerabilities in parsers, protocol handlers, and file format processors
Peer review — developers review each other's code for security issues, logic errors, and coding standard compliance
Formal inspection (Fagan inspection) — structured, multi-step code review process: planning, overview, preparation, inspection, rework, follow-up
Pair programming — two developers work together at one workstation; continuous real-time review
Automated code review — tools that scan code for known patterns of vulnerabilities (part of SAST)
Code review is one of the most effective methods for finding vulnerabilities early
Focus areas: input validation, authentication/authorization logic, error handling, cryptographic implementation, data handling
Identifies open-source and third-party components in the codebase
Checks known vulnerability databases (NVD, CVE) for vulnerabilities in those components
Verifies license compliance for open-source components
Critical for supply chain security — knowing what components are in your software
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — comprehensive inventory of all software components; increasingly required by regulation
Tools: Snyk, Black Duck, OWASP Dependency-Check, npm audit, pip-audit
